topics.title: Design Car Rental System
Chat / WhatsApp
topics.concepts: WebSockets, message ordering, delivery guarantees, presence
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a chat app like WhatsApp. Asha sends "Running 10 minutes late" to Bilal. Bilal's phone shows it within a second, and Asha sees one tick (sent), then two ticks (delivered), then blue ticks (read).

If Bilal's phone is off, he gets the message when it comes back online. Groups work the same way, and every chat keeps its messages in order.

## Requirements

- 1:1 and group chats (up to 1,024 members), text plus photos and videos.
- Real-time delivery when both users are online; offline users get messages on reconnect.
- Sent, delivered and read receipts; online / last-seen status.
- Messages in a chat appear in the same order for everyone, and no message is lost.
- 500 million daily users.

## Step 1: Clarify the requirements

> **💡 Tip**
> Chat interviews are about three things: keeping connections open, never losing a message, and keeping order. Steer the questions toward them.

**Candidate:** One-to-one only, or groups too?

**Interviewer:** Both. Groups have at most 1,024 members.

**Candidate:** Can one user be logged in on several devices?

**Interviewer:** Yes – a phone and a laptop, each must get every message.

**Candidate:** Do we keep chat history on the server?

**Interviewer:** Yes, so a new device can load it.

**Candidate:** Do we need end-to-end encryption?

**Interviewer:** Mention it, but focus on delivery.

**Candidate:** How fast should delivery be?

**Interviewer:** Under 200 ms when both users are online.

**Functional requirements**

1. Send text and media in 1:1 and group chats.
2. Deliver in real time to online devices; store for offline devices.
3. Sent, delivered and read receipts; online status.

**Non-functional requirements**

1. Low latency: under 200 ms when both are online.
2. No message loss; order is preserved within each chat.
3. 500 million daily users; about 100 million connected at once.

## Step 2: Estimate the scale

> **💡 Tip**
> For chat, size the open connections as well as the messages. Connections are what make this design unusual.

**Messages**

```text
Messages per day    = 500M users × 40 messages   = 20 billion
Average             = 20B / 86,400 s             ≈ 230,000 per second
Peak (×3)                                        ≈ 700,000 per second
```

What it means: one database cannot take this. Messages must be split (sharded) across many machines.

**Connections**

```text
Connected at once        ≈ 100 million
Connections per server   ≈ 100,000 (WebSockets are mostly idle)
Connection servers       = 100M / 100,000         ≈ 1,000
```

What it means: we need a large fleet of connection servers and a way to know which server each user is connected to.

**Storage**

```text
Average message     ≈ 200 bytes (text; media is stored separately)
Per day             = 20B × 200 bytes             ≈ 4 TB
Per year                                          ≈ 1.5 PB
```

What it means: message storage must be cheap and grow sideways – a wide-column store such as Cassandra fits.

## Step 3: Define the API

Chat uses a **WebSocket**: one connection that stays open so the server can push messages to the phone at any time. Messages on it are small JSON frames.

```http
SEND     { "chatId": "c-981", "clientMsgId": "7f3a…", "text": "Running 10 minutes late" }
→ ACK    { "clientMsgId": "7f3a…", "seq": 1042 }            (sent ✓)

← MESSAGE{ "chatId": "c-981", "seq": 1042, "from": "asha", "text": "…" }
DELIVERED{ "chatId": "c-981", "seq": 1042 }                 (delivered ✓✓)
READ     { "chatId": "c-981", "seq": 1042 }                 (read, blue ✓✓)

SYNC     { "chatId": "c-981", "afterSeq": 1030 }            (catch up after reconnect)
```

Photos and videos are uploaded over normal HTTP to object storage first; the chat message carries only the link.

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Explain why HTTP polling is wasteful here: the phone would ask "anything new?" every few seconds, mostly to hear "no". A WebSocket lets the server push the moment a message arrives.

## Step 4: Define the data model

| Table | Key | Fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `messages` | partition: chatId, sort: seq | messageId, senderId, clientMsgId, text or mediaUrl, sentAt |
| `chat_members` | chatId | userId, role, joinedAt |
| `device_cursor` | (userId, deviceId, chatId) | lastDeliveredSeq, lastReadSeq |
| `sessions` (Redis) | userId | list of (deviceId, connection server) |
| `presence` (Redis, with TTL) | userId | online, lastSeen |

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Store messages in Cassandra, partitioned by `chatId` and sorted by `seq`. "Give me chat c-981 after message 1030" is then a single, fast read from one partition.

## Step 5: Draw the high-level design

[![High-level design: client connections send messages to the conversation service, which commits them in order to the message store and fans them out through a delivery queue back to online connections; devices record what they received in device cursors, media goes to an object store and heartbeats update a presence cache.](designs/hld-6.svg)](designs/hld-6.svg)

**Sending a message**

1. Asha's phone sends `SEND` over its WebSocket to connection server 12.
2. The chat service checks Asha is a member, gives the message the next sequence number for this chat (1042), and saves it.
3. Only after saving does it reply `ACK` – Asha sees one tick.
4. It looks up Bilal's devices in the session store and pushes the message to their connection servers.

**Receiving it**

1. Bilal's phone gets `MESSAGE`, shows it and replies `DELIVERED`. Asha sees two ticks.
2. When Bilal opens the chat, his phone sends `READ`. Asha sees blue ticks.
3. If Bilal is offline, the message waits in the store. He gets a push notification, and on reconnect his phone sends `SYNC afterSeq=1041`.

![Animation: Asha's phone sends a message; the chat service saves it with sequence 1042 and acknowledges one tick; it pushes the message to Bilal's online phone, which reports delivered for two ticks; Bilal's laptop is offline, so it later reconnects and syncs everything after its last sequence.](learning-figures/hld-6-delivery.gif)

## Step 6: Go deep

### Which server is Bilal connected to?

Each connection server registers its users in Redis: `bilal → [(phone, server 7), (laptop, server 31)]`. The chat service looks this up and forwards the message to servers 7 and 31, which write it down the open sockets.

When a phone disconnects, the entry is removed (or expires with a short TTL), so we never push to a dead connection.

### Keeping messages in order

**Option 1: Order by the sender's clock.**

- Good: no coordination.
- Problem: phone clocks are wrong all the time; two people would see different orders.

**Option 2: One global sequence for all chats.**

- Good: total order.
- Problem: a single counter for 700,000 messages a second is a bottleneck, and nobody needs order *between* different chats.

**Option 3: A sequence number per chat, assigned by the server.**

- Good: everyone sees the same order in a chat; different chats scale independently.
- Problem: one chat's messages must go through one owner at a time (fine – one chat is small).

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Per-chat sequence numbers assigned by the server. Each chat is owned by one chat-service instance at a time (route by `hash(chatId)`), which hands out 1041, 1042, 1043….

### Never losing a message

The rule: **save first, acknowledge second**. Asha's phone keeps the message as "sending" until it gets `ACK`. If the network drops, the phone sends it again with the same `clientMsgId`.

The server keeps a unique key on `(senderId, clientMsgId)`. A retry finds the saved message and returns the same `seq` instead of storing a duplicate.

[![Sending safely: the phone sends with a client message ID; the server checks for a duplicate, assigns the next chat sequence, saves the message and only then acknowledges; a retry with the same ID returns the original sequence instead of creating a second message.](learning-figures/hld-6-send.svg)](learning-figures/hld-6-send.svg)

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Treating "written to the WebSocket" as "delivered". The bytes can sit in a buffer while the phone goes into a tunnel. Only the phone's `DELIVERED` reply proves delivery.

### Multiple devices

Each device keeps its own cursor – the last `seq` it received for each chat. Bilal's laptop, offline all day, syncs with `afterSeq` from its own cursor; it does not trust the phone's progress.

Read status is per user: when Bilal reads on his phone, both devices clear the unread badge.

### Groups

For a group of 200, the chat service saves the message once and pushes it to the 200 members' devices (fanout on write). For very large groups or channels, members instead pull from the group's message list using their cursor, so one message does not cause 100,000 pushes at once.

### Online status

Each phone sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds, which sets `presence:bilal = online` with a 60-second TTL. If heartbeats stop, the key expires and Bilal shows "last seen 9:42".

Presence is only sent to people who currently have Bilal's chat open – otherwise one user coming online would notify hundreds of contacts.

## Step 7: Find bottlenecks and failure points

| What fails | What happens | How we handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A connection server dies | 100,000 phones lose their socket | Phones reconnect to another server and `SYNC` from their cursors – nothing is lost because messages were saved first |
| ACK lost on the way back | Asha's phone retries | Same `clientMsgId` returns the original `seq`; no duplicate |
| Bilal is offline for a week | Messages pile up | They stay in the store; push notification; `SYNC` on reconnect, paged |
| A huge group message | Thousands of pushes at once | Members pull by cursor instead of fanout |
| Deploying connection servers | Every socket would drop at once | Drain servers gradually; clients reconnect with jitter |

## Putting it together

- **Send:** WebSocket → chat service → per-chat `seq` → save → ACK → push to recipients' servers.
- **Receive:** push to online devices; offline devices `SYNC` from their own cursor.
- **Scale:** ~1,000 connection servers, Redis for sessions and presence, Cassandra partitioned by chat.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**Why not HTTP long polling?** It works as a fallback, but each poll is a new request with headers and a held thread. WebSockets keep one cheap open connection that both sides can use.

**How does end-to-end encryption change the design?** The server stores and forwards encrypted bytes it cannot read. Each device has its own keys, so a message is encrypted once per recipient device. Server-side search becomes impossible.

**How do you send photos?** The phone uploads the photo to object storage using a short-lived upload link, then sends a chat message containing the link and a thumbnail.

**How do you show "typing…"?** A short-lived event pushed only to the open chat; it is never stored.

**What if two people send at the same moment?** Both go to the same chat owner, which gives them consecutive numbers. Both phones then show the server's order.

## Wrap up

We kept a WebSocket open per device, saved each message with a per-chat sequence number before acknowledging it, and let every device catch up from its own cursor.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - WebSockets let the server push; a session store says which server holds each device.
> - Save first, then acknowledge; `clientMsgId` turns retries into no-ops.
> - Order per chat with server-assigned sequence numbers, not device clocks.
> - Sent, delivered and read are three different facts, each confirmed by a reply.

## Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version covers what to do when a user is removed from a group while messages are in flight, how to repair gaps in a device's sequence, and why presence must never decide whether a message is stored.

[![Persist before acknowledging acceptance to the sender.](lessons/hld-6-flow.svg)](lessons/hld-6-flow.svg)

Further reading: [RFC 6455 – The WebSocket Protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455) and the [Signal protocol overview](https://signal.org/docs/) for end-to-end encryption.

## Closing answer

"Each device keeps a WebSocket open to a connection server, and a Redis session store records which server holds which device. When Asha sends a message, the chat service that owns the chat gives it the next per-chat sequence number, saves it in Cassandra partitioned by chat, and only then acknowledges – one tick. It pushes the message to Bilal's online devices; their delivered and read replies give two ticks and blue ticks. Offline devices sync from their own cursor on reconnect. Retries carry a client message ID, so they never create duplicates. Presence is soft state with heartbeats and a TTL."

topics.title: Spring AI Fundamentals
topics.markdown:
## Problem

You are adding AI features to an existing Spring Boot application. Your lead asks: *"What is Spring AI, how do we wire it in, and how do we avoid locking ourselves to one AI provider?"*

Build the smallest useful example – a `POST /api/explain` endpoint that explains a Java concept – and explain the Spring AI building blocks and how Spring Boot wires them together.

## Requirements

- Explain what Spring AI is and why a Java team would use it.
- Add the dependencies correctly (BOM and starter) and configure a provider.
- Explain the main abstractions: `ChatModel`, `ChatClient`, `EmbeddingModel`, `Prompt`.
- Build an endpoint with a service that uses `ChatClient`.
- Switch providers (cloud vs local Ollama) with configuration only.
- Test without calling a real model.

## Step 1: The idea in plain words

**Spring AI** is to AI models what Spring Data is to databases: one familiar, Spring-style API in front of many providers – OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Google Gemini, Amazon Bedrock, Ollama and more.

You get:

- **Portable interfaces** (`ChatModel`, `EmbeddingModel`) with one implementation per provider.
- **Auto-configuration**: add a starter and a few properties, and Spring Boot creates the beans.
- A fluent **`ChatClient`** for building prompts, plus structured output, chat memory, RAG (`VectorStore`), tool calling and observability.

> **🎯 In the interview**
> Interviewers usually ask: what `ChatModel` and `ChatClient` are and how they differ; how auto-configuration picks a model; how to switch providers; how to test AI code.

## Step 2: Add it to a Spring Boot project

Use the **BOM** (bill of materials) so all Spring AI modules have matching versions, then add **one starter per provider**:

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-ai-bom</artifactId>
      <version>1.1.8</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-model-openai</artifactId>   <!-- or ...-model-ollama -->
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

```properties
spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}
spring.ai.openai.chat.options.model=gpt-4o-mini
spring.ai.openai.chat.options.temperature=0.3
```

Keep API keys in environment variables or a secrets manager – never in Git.

**What happens at startup** – this is **auto-configuration**:

1. Spring Boot sees the OpenAI starter on the classpath and the `spring.ai.openai.*` properties.
2. It creates an `OpenAiChatModel` bean (the `ChatModel`) and, if available, an `OpenAiEmbeddingModel`.
3. It creates a `ChatClient.Builder` bean that wraps the `ChatModel`.
4. Your service asks for `ChatClient.Builder` in its constructor and builds a client.

![Animation: at startup Spring Boot finds the starter and properties, creates the provider's ChatModel bean, wraps it in a ChatClient.Builder and injects it into ExplanationService; switching the active profile to ollama swaps only the ChatModel bean.](learning-figures/ai-6-startup.gif)

[![Boot startup selects one ChatModel and injects collaborators: properties and the active profile choose either a test fixture ChatModel or an auto-configured OllamaChatModel; the ChatClient.Builder wraps the chosen model and is injected into the service.](learning-figures/ai-6-boot-wiring.svg)](learning-figures/ai-6-boot-wiring.svg)

## Step 3: The main abstractions

| Abstraction | What it is | When you use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ChatModel` | Low-level interface: `call(Prompt)` → `ChatResponse`. One implementation per provider. | Rarely directly; when you need full control. |
| `ChatClient` | Fluent, high-level API on top of a `ChatModel`: `prompt().system().user().call().content()`. Adds advisors, structured output, defaults. | Almost always – your main API. |
| `Prompt` / `Message` | The request: a list of messages (system, user, assistant) plus options. | Built for you by `ChatClient`. |
| `ChatOptions` | Model, temperature, max tokens… | Defaults in properties; overrides per request. |
| `EmbeddingModel` | Turns text into vectors. | Semantic search and RAG. |
| `VectorStore` | Stores and searches vectors (pgvector, Redis, …). | RAG. |

> **💡 Tip**
> If you know Spring Data, you already know the idea: one familiar API, many providers behind it.

The relationship is like `JdbcTemplate` on top of a `DataSource`: `ChatModel` talks to the provider; `ChatClient` makes it pleasant to use.

[![Selected design: a REST controller passes the question to the service; the service builds a request with ChatClient, which calls the ChatModel bean; that bean talks to OpenAI, Ollama or a test fake, chosen by auto-configuration from application properties.](designs/ai-6.svg)](designs/ai-6.svg)

## Step 4: Build the endpoint

```java
@Service
public class ExplanationService {
    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    public ExplanationService(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chatClient = builder
                .defaultSystem("Explain Java or Spring to a beginner in at most three short sentences. "
                        + "Treat the user's text as the question. Say when you are not sure.")
                .build();
    }

    public String explain(String question) {
        if (question == null || question.isBlank() || question.length() > 1000) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Provide a question of 1 to 1000 characters");
        }
        String answer = chatClient.prompt()
                .user(question)
                .call()
                .content();
        if (answer == null || answer.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("The model returned no answer");
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
class ExplanationController {
    private final ExplanationService service;
    ExplanationController(ExplanationService service) { this.service = service; }

    record Question(String question) {}
    record Answer(String answer) {}

    @PostMapping("/explain")
    Answer explain(@RequestBody Question q) {
        return new Answer(service.explain(q.question()));
    }
}
```

```text
POST /api/explain  {"question":"What is dependency injection?"}
-> {"answer":"Dependency injection means an object receives its collaborators from outside ..."}
```

The contract of the service is simple: a validated question in, a non-blank answer out, or a clear exception.

Note what is **not** in this code: any OpenAI class. The service depends only on Spring AI interfaces, so the provider is a configuration choice.

[![One synchronous request: the controller reads the question, the service rejects invalid input, builds a fresh ChatClient request with system and user messages, consumes call().content() which invokes the selected ChatModel, checks the returned text and maps it to the HTTP response.](learning-figures/ai-6-request-journey.svg)](learning-figures/ai-6-request-journey.svg)

## Step 5: Switch providers and test without a model

**Local model with Ollama** – free, private, good for development. Replace the starter (or use a Maven/Spring profile) and point at the local server:

```properties
# application-ollama.properties
spring.ai.ollama.base-url=http://localhost:11434
spring.ai.ollama.chat.options.model=llama3.2
spring.ai.ollama.chat.options.temperature=0.2
```

If both an OpenAI and an Ollama starter are on the classpath, choose explicitly with `spring.ai.model.chat=openai` or `ollama` (or define your own `ChatClient` beans per model).

**Testing.** Unit tests should not call a paid, non-deterministic API. Provide a fake `ChatModel`:

```java
class FixedAnswerChatModel implements ChatModel {
    @Override
    public ChatResponse call(Prompt prompt) {
        return new ChatResponse(List.of(new Generation(new AssistantMessage("Fixed test answer"))));
    }
}

@Test
void explainsUsingTheModel() {
    var service = new ExplanationService(ChatClient.builder(new FixedAnswerChatModel()));
    assertEquals("Fixed test answer", service.explain("What is DI?"));
}

@Test
void rejectsBlankQuestion() {
    var service = new ExplanationService(ChatClient.builder(new FixedAnswerChatModel()));
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> service.explain(" "));
}
```

Test **your** logic – validation, prompt building, error handling – with the fake. Check model quality separately with a small evaluation set against the real model.

**When something breaks, check in this order:** is the starter on the classpath → are the properties and API key set → is the right profile active → can the app reach the provider (network, proxy) → is the model name valid → did the call time out.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**`ChatModel` vs `ChatClient`?** `ChatModel` is the low-level, provider-specific implementation of a common interface. `ChatClient` is the fluent API built on it, adding system defaults, advisors (memory, RAG, logging), structured output and streaming.

**How do you use two different models in one app?** Create two `ChatClient` beans, each built from a different `ChatModel` (for example a cheap model for classification and a stronger one for answers), and inject them with qualifiers.

**Is Spring AI only for OpenAI?** No – it supports many providers through the same interfaces, including local models via Ollama.

**Should the controller call `ChatClient` directly?** Better in a service: validation, prompts and error handling stay testable and reusable.

**How do you handle provider errors?** Spring AI has built-in retries (`spring.ai.retry.*`) for transient errors; add timeouts, map failures to clear HTTP errors (e.g. 503), and log usage.

**How do you observe AI calls?** Spring AI integrates with Micrometer: it records latency and token usage metrics and traces for model calls.

## Wrap up

Spring AI gives one Spring-style API over many AI providers; auto-configuration wires the `ChatModel` and `ChatClient.Builder` from a starter and properties.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Import the BOM, add one provider starter, set properties.
> - `ChatModel` is the provider interface; `ChatClient` is the fluent API you use.
> - Depend only on Spring AI interfaces so switching providers is configuration.
> - Unit-test with a fake `ChatModel`; evaluate the real model separately.

## Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version follows auto-configuration step by step (BOM vs starter, conditional bean creation, profiles), shows exactly which boundary to inspect first when something breaks, and ships a complete runnable project that works offline with a fixture model and against a local Ollama model with one profile switch.

[Open the Spring wiring lab](learning-labs/spring-fundamentals.html), download the [complete project](reference-code/learning/spring-fundamentals.zip), or read its [focused tests](reference-code/learning/spring-fundamentals/src/test/java/kb/springfundamentals/FundamentalsTest.java). See the [Spring AI reference documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/) for supported providers.

## Closing answer

"Spring AI gives Java teams one Spring-style API over many AI providers. I import the Spring AI BOM and add one provider starter; auto-configuration creates the provider's `ChatModel` and a `ChatClient.Builder` from properties. My service injects the builder, sets a default system prompt and calls `chatClient.prompt().user(question).call().content()`. Because the code depends only on Spring AI interfaces, switching from OpenAI to a local Ollama model is a configuration change. `ChatModel` is the low-level provider interface, `ChatClient` the fluent API with advisors and structured output, and `EmbeddingModel` and `VectorStore` support RAG. I unit-test with a fake `ChatModel` and evaluate real model quality separately."
